Medgar Evers. A field organizer for the NAACP in Mississippi and one of the most effective civil rights leaders of the nineteen-sixties, orchestrating campaigns for desegregation and voting rights in one of the most hostile environments in the South. From 1954 onward he served as the NAACP state field secretary for Mississippi, making him the face of the organization in the state's most dangerous terrain. In 1962 he led campaigns to desegregate the University of Mississippi, supporting James Meredith through court battles and subsequent enrollment. He organized voter registration drives throughout Mississippi, personally recruiting and training volunteers despite severe risks. He mentored younger activists and SNCC workers, providing strategic guidance and emotional support through years of constant danger. On June 12, 1963 he was assassinated outside his home by Byron De La Beckwith, a white supremacist. The murder occurred just after President Kennedy's civil rights address to the nation. His death brought Mississippi's racial violence to the center of national attention and accelerated calls for federal intervention in the South. His murderer evaded conviction for over thirty years before being retried and convicted in 1994, a delayed justice that became symbolic of the long struggle for accountability. He shared the cause that Martin Luther King Jr. led, though Evers worked at the grassroots level where the real risks were greatest. Like Rosa Parks, he became a martyr in spirit to the movement, both becoming sacred names. He was part of the same generation as John Lewis, younger activists facing similar dangers, and he exemplified the kind of grassroots, frontline commitment to community power that Ella Baker valorized.
